The study focused on simulating two-dimensional transient buoyant plume flows.
The computational domain was a 1 m x 1 m rectangular enclosure filled with air at a reference temperature of 293.15 K.
Warm air at a temperature of 303.15 K was blown into the domain through a fixed uniform inlet velocity of 0.125 m/s.
A uniform Cartesian grid with 256 cells per meter was used for spatial discretization.
The simulations were run without turbulence modeling, and a first-order backward Euler time integration scheme was used.
The Poisson equation for pressure correction can consume up to 80% of the computational time in incompressible fluid flow simulations.
The hybrid approach used a fully connected neural network to predict the pressure field at the cell level.
The predicted pressure field was used as an initial guess to solve the Poisson equation, accelerating the pressure-velocity coupling procedure.
The results showed an average improvement of 94% in the initial guess for solving the Poisson equation.
The first pressure corrector acceleration reached a mean factor of 3, depending on the iterative solver employed.
The hybrid approach was evaluated on various geometries and initial conditions without additional training.
The study aimed to develop a versatile, scalable, accurate, robust, and data-efficient hybrid CFD/machine learning methodology.
The hybrid approach is designed to enhance the efficiency of CFD iterative linear solvers while maintaining physical consistency.
The study focused on buoyant plume simulations, but the hybrid approach could be applied to other fluid flow domains.
The open-source CFD software OpenFOAM was used to simulate the transient buoyant plume flows.
